removed.title: Health Fair Stall Cards
removed.text:
STALL 1 — Voice Check Corner
Offers: a microphone and a simple pitch meter for fun.
Visitor: Arjun, 13, notices his voice crackles when he speaks into the mic and sees a slight bulge at his throat in the mirror next to the stall.

STALL 2 — Cycle Calendar Stall
Offers: menstrual tracking charts and information on hygiene products.
Visitor: Meena, 12, recently started her periods and wants to understand the cycle length and what products she can use.

STALL 3 — Iron-Strong Station
Offers: a display of iron-rich foods (spinach, kidney beans, dried fruits) and a quiz.
Visitor: Priya, 14, often feels tired; the stall helper asks whether her periods have started recently.

STALL 4 — Move and Mood Zone
Offers: short group dance and sport sessions.
Visitor: Rahul, 13, came because he has been feeling irritable at home and his friend suggested this stall.

STALL 5 — Why Is This Happening? Corner
Offers: a short talk with an illustrated chart of the brain-signal chain.
Visitor: Divya, 11, wants to know why so many changes are happening to her body all at once.

STALL 6 — Choose Strong Stall
Offers: role-play cards where visitors practise refusing peer pressure to try tobacco or alcohol.
Visitor: Karan, 15, says some friends have been pressuring him at school.

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe physical changes of adolescence
periods.activity_description: Students anonymously write changes they observe in peers from Grades 5 to 8 — in height, strength, voice, facial features, and appearance — on slips of paper. Slips are pooled and sorted into categories on the board, generating a class-wide picture of adolescent change.

roles.role_description: Facilitates the anonymous slip collection, sorts categories on the board, and draws out the most frequently noted changes.
Writes observations on slips independently before contributing to the group sort.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's opening scenario — Venkatesh and Devyani noticing changes in each other — and poses the guiding question: what kinds of changes happen as children grow into adults?
Students individually write anonymous observations of changes they notice in peers across grade levels on slips of paper, which are folded and placed in a container.
Teacher draws slips randomly and sorts the observations into emerging categories (height, voice, body structure, facial features, skin, behaviour) on the board with student input.
Class identifies the most commonly noted changes and teacher introduces the term adolescence and its approximate age span of 10 to 19 years.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit orients students to the chapter's central subject — the changes of adolescence — using the chapter's own Activity 6.1. Watch for students who conflate changes that are purely social or cultural with biological ones; gently steer the category sort toward observable physical changes without dismissing other entries. If the class is hesitant to write personal observations, reassure them that anonymity is real and that no slip will be read aloud with any student's name attached.
materials: Container or jar for collecting slips

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe physical changes of adolescence
periods.activity_title: Mapping the Body: Secondary Sexual Characteristics Chart
periods.activity_description: Working in same-gender pairs, students complete a structured observation chart distinguishing physical changes common to both boys and girls from those specific to each. They use chapter text and the previous unit's sorted categories as source material, producing a two-column annotated chart.

roles.role_description: Circulates to ensure accurate recording, clarifies the distinction between primary and secondary sexual characteristics, and manages a sensitive classroom environment.
Collaboratively complete the observation chart, classifying changes and annotating with brief explanations of what causes each visible change (e.g., larynx growth → voice change).

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the category sort from the previous unit and introduces the term secondary sexual characteristics, explaining what makes a characteristic 'secondary'.
Pairs work through the chapter text to populate a three-column chart: change observed, who it affects (both / boys only / girls only), and the body structure responsible.
Pairs compare charts across the class; teacher consolidates a master version on the board, correcting any misclassifications (e.g., voice box growth affecting both sexes but to different degrees).
Teacher highlights the skin and acne connection — increased oily secretions — as one concrete mechanism linking body change to observable appearance.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the previous unit's sorted categories, now asking students to go a step further and name the responsible body structure for each change. A common error is to list acne as a change unique to boys; the chapter is clear it affects both sexes, driven by increased oily secretions in skin pores. Keep the classroom tone matter-of-fact and scientific throughout — the chart format itself helps by framing these changes as data rather than personal commentary.

periods.stage_label: Classify and explain reproductive maturation changes
periods.activity_title: Inside the Change: Reproductive Maturation and the Menstrual Cycle
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of statements about internal adolescent changes and sort them into 'external/visible' and 'internal/reproductive' categories, then investigate the menstrual cycle's timeline by placing key events on a 28–30 day cycle strip, distinguishing menstruation from the broader cycle.

roles.role_description: Poses the inquiry question — what changes happen inside the body that we cannot directly see? — and guides students through the cycle-strip task.
Sort statement cards and complete the cycle-strip timeline, justifying their placements to group members.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the inquiry question and distributes statement cards; groups sort cards into external and internal categories and briefly justify their groupings.
Teacher introduces the menstrual cycle timeline; groups place key phases (menstruation, cycle duration, age of onset, age of natural end) on a numbered cycle strip.
Groups share their cycle strips; teacher facilitates a comparison, noting the healthy range of 21 to 35 days and the 3 to 7 day duration of menstruation itself.
Class examines the 'Breaking Myths' box together; students identify one myth and its scientific rebuttal as a closing check.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit shifts from visible to internal changes, a cognitive step that requires students to reason about processes they cannot directly observe. A frequent confusion is treating the entire menstrual cycle as synonymous with menstruation; the cycle-strip task is designed to make the distinction concrete. When reviewing the myths box, model a calm, factual tone — this content may be sensitive for some students, and framing it as standard biological science helps normalise it.
materials: Printed or handwritten statement cards (one set per group)

periods.stage_label: Classify and explain reproductive maturation changes
periods.activity_title: Puberty Defined: Connecting Visible and Internal Change
periods.activity_description: Teacher-led structured explanation consolidates the distinction between puberty (external and internal changes that prepare the body for reproduction) and secondary sexual characteristics (externally visible differentiators not directly involved in reproduction). Students construct a concept map linking puberty, secondary sexual characteristics, the menstrual cycle, and adolescence.

roles.role_description: Delivers a structured explanation of the two key definitions and their relationship, drawing on the sorted chart and cycle strip produced in earlier units.
Constructs a personal concept map connecting the four key terms using arrows and brief link labels.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains and contrasts puberty and secondary sexual characteristics using examples from the chart built in the previous unit, making explicit which changes fall under each definition.
Students individually draft a concept map placing adolescence, puberty, secondary sexual characteristics, and the menstrual cycle as nodes, with labelled arrows showing how they relate.
Two or three volunteers share their maps; class identifies which links are consistently drawn and where differences appear, with teacher clarifying any misconceptions.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the classification work of the previous two units by asking students to hold multiple definitions simultaneously and show relationships between them — a step up from sorting. Watch for concept maps that place menstruation as a cause of puberty rather than as a change that occurs during puberty; correct this by returning to the cycle-strip evidence. The concept map is also a useful checkpoint: a student who can draw correct directional arrows between all four nodes has genuinely distinguished the terms.
materials: Blank A4 paper or notebook pages for concept maps

periods.stage_label: Analyse emotional and behavioural change as linked phenomena
periods.activity_description: Students reflect on emotional and behavioural changes during adolescence, complete a structured three-column table identifying an emotional change, its probable effect on behaviour, and a constructive channel for that energy, then examine patterns across the class to identify which emotions are most commonly reported.

roles.role_description: Introduces the inquiry frame — that emotions and behaviours are linked, not random — and facilitates the whole-class pattern discussion.
Independently completes the three-column table before sharing one entry with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous unit's concept map by asking: puberty accounts for physical changes — what drives emotional shifts? Students hypothesise briefly.

Students individually complete the three-column table (emotional change / probable behavioural effect / constructive channel), drawing on their own experience and the chapter's examples such as music, dance, and sports.
Teacher tallies the most commonly entered emotional changes on the board and the class examines whether the same emotion can produce different behavioural effects depending on how it is channelled.
Teacher introduces the key idea: that understanding the emotion–behaviour link is itself a skill that helps adolescents respond thoughtfully rather than react impulsively.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens a new progression stage, moving from classifying changes to analysing how two types of change — emotional and behavioural — are causally linked to each other. A common error is listing behaviour as the emotion itself (e.g., writing 'anger' in both columns); probe with the question 'what might someone do when they feel this?' to push toward the effect column. The tally on the board often reveals that mood swings and heightened sensitivity are near-universal, which normalises the experience for students who feel these changes are unusual.
materials: Notebook pages or printed Table 6.2 template

periods.stage_label: Analyse emotional and behavioural change as linked phenomena
periods.activity_title: Wellness Audit: Nutrition, Hygiene, and Activity During Adolescence
periods.activity_description: Student groups receive scenario cards describing an adolescent's daily choices across nutrition, hygiene, and physical activity; they audit each scenario against chapter-specified needs (calcium, iron, protein sources; hygiene practices; exercise) and record which needs are met, which are unmet, and what the likely consequence is.

roles.role_description: Distributes scenario cards, frames the task as a scientific audit rather than a moral judgement, and consolidates findings.
Works through each scenario card, cross-referencing against the chapter's nutritional and hygiene guidance to complete an audit record.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the emotion-behaviour analysis: adolescents who meet their physical wellness needs are better placed to manage emotional change — framing wellness as a coherent system.

Groups receive two scenario cards each and complete an audit table: need identified, present or absent in the scenario, and likely health consequence drawn from chapter content (e.g., iron deficiency → blood-related health problems).
Groups report one finding each; class compares which unmet needs appear most frequently and which chapter-specified foods or practices would address them.
Teacher highlights the iron and Vitamin B12 note for adolescent girls and the Dorothy Hodgkin feature as a brief factual close.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the analysis stage by asking students to reason about consequences of unmet needs — a step beyond simply listing what adolescents should eat or do. A frequent error is confusing protein sources with calcium sources; the audit format exposes this because students must match each food to the specific need it meets. The scenario card format keeps the analysis grounded in concrete situations rather than abstract lists, which aligns with how the chapter presents this content.
materials: Scenario cards (teacher-prepared, drawn from section 6.4 content)

periods.stage_label: Analyse emotional and behavioural change as linked phenomena
periods.activity_title: Responsible Choices: Social Media Dos and Don'ts Poster
periods.activity_description: Groups design a poster or pamphlet about responsible social media behaviour and cyberbullying prevention, completing the chapter's dos and don'ts table and translating it into a visual format that could be displayed in a school corridor. Groups also incorporate the chapter's definition of cyberbullying and at least one recommended response strategy.

roles.role_description: Frames the task as an application of the chapter's balanced social life guidance and circulates to ensure posters reflect chapter content rather than general opinion.
Designs the poster collaboratively, first completing the dos and don'ts table from chapter text, then translating it into a visual product.

time_bands.activity: Teacher links this unit to the previous unit's wellness audit: just as physical wellness requires specific practices, social wellness has its own set of evidence-based behaviours from the chapter.

Groups complete the dos and don'ts table using section 6.4.4, then design a poster or pamphlet layout that communicates cyberbullying's definition, one real consequence, and at least two recommended actions from the chapter.
Groups display their posters and conduct a brief gallery walk; peers identify one strong feature and one gap in each poster's coverage of chapter content.
Teacher draws attention to the chapter's advice to seek help from parents or teachers rather than respond with fear — highlighting this as an evidence-based coping strategy.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the analysis stage by asking students to translate chapter guidance into a communicable product, which requires them to make judgements about what is most important to convey. Watch for posters that add personal opinions about social media not grounded in the chapter; redirect these by asking which part of the chapter supports that claim. The gallery walk functions as a peer-review checkpoint — students who can identify a gap in another group's poster are demonstrating that they themselves know what the chapter requires.
materials: Chart paper or A3 paper for posters

periods.stage_label: Explain hormones as the biological cause underlying all adolescent changes
periods.activity_title: The 'Why' Behind the Changes: Introducing Hormones
periods.activity_description: Teacher delivers a structured explanation of hormones — chemical substances produced in the body, released on signals from the brain — and their role in driving puberty, the menstrual cycle, and mood changes. Students then annotate a blank body outline diagram, labelling where hormonal signals originate and what changes they produce.

roles.role_description: Delivers the explanation of hormones and their mechanism, explicitly connecting each hormone-driven change back to changes students classified in earlier units.
Annotates a body outline diagram with arrows showing hormone origin (brain signal), production site, and the change produced.

time_bands.activity: Teacher delivers a structured explanation of what hormones are, how the brain sends signals for their release, and why this mechanism accounts for the changes mapped in the class chart and concept map from earlier units.

Students annotate a blank body outline: drawing an arrow from the brain outward, labelling hormone production as the mechanism, and connecting each arrow to the specific change it drives (height, voice, menstrual cycle, mood).
Students compare annotated diagrams in pairs and identify any change from earlier units that they have not yet connected to a hormonal signal.
Teacher consolidates: all changes covered in this chapter — physical, reproductive, and emotional — trace back to hormonal activity, framing section 6.5 as the chapter's explanatory core.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's highest-order stage by introducing hormones as the unifying causal explanation for everything students have observed and classified so far. A common misconception is that only physical changes are hormone-driven, while mood swings are 'just feelings'; the chapter explicitly states that mood changes during adolescence are primarily driven by hormonal activity, so challenge this if it arises. The body-outline annotation works best when students are encouraged to draw arrows from the concept map they built in an earlier unit, making the causal chain visible.
materials: Blank body outline diagram (one per student, teacher-prepared)

periods.stage_label: Explain hormones as the biological cause underlying all adolescent changes
periods.activity_title: Substance Harm and Hormonal Disruption: Saying No with Reasons
periods.activity_description: Students examine the chapter's list of harmful substances and their health consequences, then construct a causal chain explaining why substance abuse during adolescence is especially damaging: the body is undergoing rapid hormonal change, and harmful substances interfere with health at this critical stage. Groups write a short evidence-based argument a peer could use to decline a substance.

roles.role_description: Frames the inquiry question — why might these substances be particularly harmful during adolescence specifically? — and monitors that arguments are grounded in chapter evidence.
Builds a causal chain from substance ingestion to health consequence, then drafts a peer-dialogue argument using chapter-specified evidence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the inquiry question and connects it to the previous unit: if hormones regulate growth and development, what happens when harmful substances interfere with the body during this period?

Groups list each substance from section 6.4.5 alongside its chapter-specified consequence (breathing difficulties, memory loss, lung damage) and construct a causal chain: substance → physiological effect → impact on adolescent development.
Groups draft a short, evidence-based peer dialogue — a confident, reasoned refusal that names at least one specific health consequence from the chapter.
Two groups share their dialogues; class evaluates whether the refusal is grounded in biological evidence from the chapter or relies on general statements.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the causal explanation stage by asking students to apply hormonal reasoning to substance harm — moving from describing consequences to explaining why adolescence is a particularly vulnerable period. Watch for arguments that are purely social or moral ('it's wrong') rather than biological; redirect by asking which health consequence from the chapter they can cite. The peer-dialogue format gives the reasoning a real-world application without leaving the chapter's content domain.
materials: Notebook pages for causal chain and dialogue draft

periods.stage_label: Explain hormones as the biological cause underlying all adolescent changes
periods.activity_title: Government Schemes as Evidence: Connecting Biology to Public Health Policy
periods.activity_description: Students map each government scheme mentioned in the chapter (MHS, RKSK, Suvidha, Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, nutritional schemes) to the specific biological need it addresses, producing a two-column evidence table that shows how each scheme responds to a chapter-identified health consequence of adolescence.

roles.role_description: Frames this as a causal analysis task — each scheme exists because adolescence creates a specific biological vulnerability — and consolidates the class table.
Searches the chapter for each scheme, identifies the biological need it addresses, and records both in the evidence table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the causal chain work of the previous unit: governments design health schemes in response to biological evidence — today's task is to trace that evidence backward from policy to biology.

Groups work through each Science and Society box in the chapter, recording the scheme name, what it provides or promotes, and the specific biological vulnerability (iron deficiency, menstrual hygiene, substance addiction) it targets.

Class constructs a master evidence table on the board; teacher draws attention to the fact that multiple schemes target adolescent girls specifically, connecting this to the chapter's note on iron and Vitamin B12 deficiency.
Teacher closes by framing this unit as proof that the biological changes of adolescence are significant enough to drive national public health responses — completing the causal arc.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the causal explanation stage by connecting hormonal and biological changes to real-world policy responses, a move that requires students to reason about why a scheme exists rather than simply describing what it does. A common error is listing a scheme's features without connecting it to a biological cause; push groups to name the specific chapter-stated health consequence that the scheme responds to. This unit closes the arc before the synthesis unit and should leave students with a clear sense that the chapter's biology and its social content are causally connected, not separate topics.
materials: Chapter text (all Science and Society boxes)
Notebook pages for group evidence tables

periods.stage_label: Explain hormones as the biological cause underlying all adolescent changes

roles.role_description: Distributes scenario cards, facilitates the whole-class convergence discussion, and draws the chapter's causal chain to a close on the board.
Analyses each scenario card by identifying the biological cause, the observable change, and the well-being implication, then presents the chain to the class.

periods.activity_title: Adolescence on the Ground: Tracing Biology Through a Community Health Fair
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of six information cards describing a fictional community health fair organised for adolescents. Each card presents a stall at the fair — its name, what it offers, and a brief profile of one adolescent visitor — without labelling the biology. Working in groups, students build a wall chart that maps each stall and visitor profile to the biological changes, hormonal drivers, and well-being measures covered in the chapter, then identify one stall that addresses more than one change at once and explain why that overlap exists. The completed charts reveal the chapter's full architecture — physical, reproductive, emotional, and well-being dimensions — held together by hormonal causation.
periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit uses a fictional community health fair to let groups map every domain of the chapter — physical, reproductive, emotional, and well-being — onto a single spatial artefact, revealing hormonal causation as the thread connecting all six stalls. The critical facilitation move during group work is pushing any group that writes only 'hormones' in the driver column to name the specific signal, effect, and change; the stall card descriptions and blank wall-chart template are ready to project or distribute (see materials and visual aids).
materials: Six stall cards per group, one card per stall (see visual aid: 'Health Fair Stall Cards')
One large sheet of chart paper per group
Markers (at least two colours per group)
Blank wall-chart template pre-drawn on the board (see visual aid: 'Wall-Chart Template')
Student notebooks (for individual jottings before group discussion)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the setting: 'Imagine your district has organised a one-day health fair specifically for adolescents aged 10–19. Six stalls have been set up, each addressing something happening in adolescent bodies or lives. Your group receives six cards — one per stall — each describing what the stall offers and one visitor who stopped there. Your job is not to design the fair; the fair already exists. Your job is to explain it — to show that you can read each stall and visitor profile and identify exactly which biological change, which hormonal driver, and which well-being measure from our chapter it connects to.' Teacher projects or writes the four-column wall-chart structure on the board, then distributes the stall cards face-down. Groups may not flip the cards until the signal. Teacher reads aloud Stall 1 as a worked example: 'Stall 1 — Voice Check Corner. Offers: a microphone and a simple pitch meter for fun. Visitor: Arjun, 13, notices his voice crackles when he speaks into the mic and he sees a slight bulge at his throat in the mirror next to the stall.' Teacher asks: 'What column entries would you write for Stall 1?' Takes two or three quick responses from the class to model the task, then signals groups to flip their cards.

Groups work through all six stall cards, filling in their wall chart. The stall cards read as follows — Stall 2: Cycle Calendar Stall, offers menstrual tracking charts and information on hygiene products; visitor Meena, 12, recently started her periods and wants to understand the cycle length and what products she can use. Stall 3: Iron-Strong Station, offers a display of iron-rich foods (spinach, kidney beans, dried fruits) and a quiz; visitor Priya, 14, often feels tired and the stall helper asks whether her periods have started recently. Stall 4: Move and Mood Zone, offers short group dance and sport sessions; visitor Rahul, 13, came because he has been feeling irritable at home and his friend suggested this stall. Stall 5: Why Is This Happening? Corner, offers a short talk with an illustrated chart of the brain-signal chain; visitor Divya, 11, wants to know why so many changes are happening to her body all at once. Stall 6: Choose Strong Stall, offers role-play cards where visitors practise refusing peer pressure to try tobacco or alcohol; visitor Karan, 15, says some friends have been pressuring him at school. Groups must complete all four columns for all six stalls; for Stall 3 they must additionally answer in a fifth row: 'Why does this stall overlap with Stall 2? Write one sentence using biology, not common sense.' Teacher circulates, prompting groups who write vague hormonal drivers to be specific about the chain from brain signal to effect.

Each group nominates one member to present the overlap answer — the connection between Iron-Strong Station and Cycle Calendar Stall — while the rest of the class listens and checks their own chart. After three groups share (in rapid succession, one sentence each), teacher opens a whole-class check on two columns most likely to be imprecise: 'Hormonal Driver' and 'Well-Being Measure Addressed'. For each, teacher invites a group to read their entry aloud, and the class gives a thumbs-up or a silent correction written in notebooks. Teacher draws attention to Stall 4 (Move and Mood Zone) as the case where emotional change and physical activity intersect — asking: 'Why does channelling emotion through physical activity appear at an adolescent health fair rather than a children's fair?' Elicits: rapid hormonal changes produce mood swings; physical activity is a constructive channel specific to this stage.

Teacher steps back from the wall charts and addresses the class directly: 'Look at your chart. You just explained an entire health fair using one chapter. Every stall made sense because the chapter gave you a connected explanation — not six separate facts, but one system: hormones drive physical, reproductive, and emotional changes; those changes create specific needs; well-being measures answer those needs with biological reasons. That is what this chapter taught. The fair worked because the biology works.' Teacher invites one student to name the single concept that runs through every row of the chart. Expected response: hormones, or the hormonal explanation. Teacher closes: 'Adolescence is not a collection of problems to manage — it is a stage with an explanation, and now you have it.'

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and describe physical changes of adolescence
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe, anonymously record, and classify the visible physical changes of adolescence — height, voice, body structure, facial hair, skin — into a structured chart distinguishing changes common to both sexes from those specific to each, and identify the body structure responsible for each change.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can describe the observable physical changes that occur during adolescence, classify them by who they affect, and name the body structure responsible for each change.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and explain reproductive maturation changes
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sort internal and external adolescent changes, map the menstrual cycle timeline, distinguish menstruation from the full cycle, and construct a concept map that correctly relates adolescence, puberty, secondary sexual characteristics, and the menstrual cycle.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can distinguish internal reproductive maturation changes from external physical changes, accurately describe the menstrual cycle's duration and phases, and correctly relate the terms puberty, secondary sexual characteristics, and adolescence in a concept map.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Analyse emotional and behavioural change as linked phenomena
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse how emotions and behaviours are causally linked during adolescence, audit scenarios against chapter-specified nutritional and hygiene needs, and design a poster translating the chapter's social wellness guidance into a communicable product.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can analyse how emotional changes during adolescence lead to specific behavioural effects, identify measures for meeting nutritional, hygiene, and social well-being needs, and justify these measures using evidence from the chapter.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain hormones as the biological cause underlying all adolescent changes
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students receive an explanation of hormones as the unifying causal mechanism, annotate body diagrams tracing hormonal signals to specific changes, construct causal chains connecting substance harm to adolescent biological vulnerability, map government schemes to the biological needs they address, and finally synthesise the full chapter by tracing any adolescent situation from biological root through observable change to well-being implication.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can describe how hormonal signals from the brain drive the physical, reproductive, and emotional changes of adolescence, and identify specific measures — dietary, hygienic, social, and policy-level — that support well-being during this stage.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe physical changes of adolescence
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can describe the observable physical changes that occur during adolescence, classify them by who they affect, and name the body structure responsible for each change.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological changes (growth, hormonal) during adolescence and measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: During adolescence, both boys and girls develop hair in the armpits and pubic region, but only boys develop moustaches and beards. Which statement correctly explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Boys and girls both grow facial hair, but girls remove it more frequently.

options.label: B
options.text: Facial hair growth in boys is caused by the growth of the voice box during adolescence.

options.label: C
options.text: Facial hair in boys is a secondary sexual characteristic, while underarm and pubic hair growth is common to both sexes.

options.label: D
options.text: Underarm hair is a primary sexual characteristic and facial hair is unrelated to adolescence.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates a social misconception about hair removal rather than a biological distinction; the student has not engaged with the chapter's classification of secondary sexual characteristics.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses primary and secondary sexual characteristics; the student has not applied the chapter's definition, which reserves 'primary' for structures directly involved in reproduction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses two separate mechanisms — larynx growth (voice change) and hormonal influence on hair distribution — conflating two distinct changes from the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the terminology may still demonstrate understanding by describing the difference in their own words before matching to the correct option. Verbal explanation alongside written choice is a valid pathway.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe physical changes of adolescence
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can describe the observable physical changes that occur during adolescence, classify them by who they affect, and name the body structure responsible for each change.

competency.competency_text: Describing biological changes (growth, hormonal) during adolescence and measures to ensure overall well-being.

assessment_items.question_text: Aarav notices his voice has become hoarse and he can see a visible bump at the front of his throat. What is the correct explanation for both observations?

options.label: A
options.text: Girls experience the same voice change and Adam's apple as boys, since the larynx grows equally in both sexes.

options.label: B
options.text: His vocal cords have been damaged by frequent loud speaking, causing both the hoarseness and the bump.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased oily secretions from skin pores during adolescence cause the bump, which is a form of acne near the throat.

options.label: D
options.text: The growth of the larynx (voice box) during adolescence produces a deeper, hoarse voice and is visible as the Adam's apple.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Attributes the change to behaviour (loud speaking) rather than biological development — a misconception not grounded in chapter content, suggesting the student has not engaged with the larynx explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses two distinct adolescent changes — acne (caused by oily secretions) and voice change (caused by larynx growth) — by incorrectly applying the acne mechanism to the throat.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misapplies the chapter's statement that both sexes experience larynx growth by ignoring the chapter's explicit note that boys experience more prominent change, including the visible Adam's apple.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find multiple-choice format constraining may be invited to explain the two observations verbally to the teacher before selecting an option, confirming that understanding rather than test-format fluency is being assessed.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Menstruation and the menstrual cycle are the same thing.' Which response correctly addresses this statement?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct — menstruation and the menstrual cycle both begin at puberty and end at the same time, so the terms are interchangeable.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is correct — menstruation refers to the entire 28 to 30 day process of the reproductive cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is incorrect — menstruation is a continuous process that lasts from puberty through adulthood without recurring cycles.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is incorrect — the menstrual cycle is the full recurring cycle of approximately 28 to 30 days, while menstruation is specifically the phase of blood discharge lasting three to seven days within that cycle.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates the part (menstruation) with the whole (menstrual cycle) — the most common confusion this question is designed to surface.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misunderstands the recurring, cyclical nature of menstruation, replacing it with a continuous-process model that has no basis in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Correctly identifies that both begin at puberty and end at a similar time, but incorrectly concludes that shared timing makes the terms interchangeable — a partial-knowledge error.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who have been told that discussing menstruation is taboo may feel reluctant to engage; teachers may allow written responses rather than verbal ones. The question is framed as a factual correction task, which reduces personal exposure.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya is 11 years old and has recently started experiencing the onset of the menstrual cycle. Her friend says this means Priya has entered adulthood. Which classification correctly describes Priya's stage and the nature of this change?

options.label: A
options.text: Priya has entered adolescence only because of the menstrual cycle; without it, she would still be in childhood regardless of age.

options.label: B
options.text: Priya has entered adulthood because the menstrual cycle is a primary sexual characteristic that only occurs after the body is fully adult.

options.label: C
options.text: Priya is in adolescence, and the menstrual cycle is a secondary sexual characteristic because it is an external change visible to others.

options.label: D
options.text: Priya is in adolescence; the onset of the menstrual cycle is an internal change associated with puberty — the stage within adolescence when the body develops the capability for reproduction.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misclassifies puberty-stage changes as markers of full adulthood, and incorrectly labels the menstrual cycle as a primary sexual characteristic — a double classification error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly places Priya in adolescence but misclassifies the menstrual cycle as a secondary sexual characteristic, confusing the chapter's distinction between external (secondary) and internal (reproductive maturation) changes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces adolescence to a single biological marker, ignoring the chapter's definition of adolescence as spanning ages 10–19 and encompassing multiple types of change.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may approach this via the concept map built in class — tracing where 'menstrual cycle' and 'puberty' sit relative to 'adolescence' is an equivalent reasoning pathway. Teachers may accept a labelled diagram as an alternative response.

assessment_items.question_text: A student's notes say: 'Puberty means adolescence.' Explain in two to three sentences why this is not accurate, using the correct relationship between the two terms and giving one example of a change that is part of puberty.
expected_elements: Adolescence is the broader stage of development between childhood and adulthood, generally spanning ages 10 to 19.
Puberty is a specific stage within adolescence during which the body undergoes external and internal changes to develop into an adult capable of reproduction.
At least one specific change associated with puberty is cited — for example, onset of the menstrual cycle, growth of the larynx, or development of secondary sexual characteristics.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya, aged 13, frequently experiences mood swings and finds herself withdrawing from friends. According to the chapter's framework, which response best describes what is happening and how she could channel this change constructively?

options.label: A
options.text: Mood swings during adolescence are a physical change, not an emotional one, and are treated the same way as voice changes or height increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Riya is experiencing heightened emotions typical of adolescence; channelling this energy through music, sports, or creative activities can help her manage these emotions constructively.

options.label: C
options.text: Riya's behaviour is caused only by poor nutrition, and correcting her iron intake will resolve the mood swings.

options.label: D
options.text: Riya's mood swings are a sign of a personality disorder and she should avoid social situations until she feels better.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Medicalises a normal developmental process, showing the student has not engaged with the chapter's framing of mood swings as a typical and manageable aspect of adolescence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reduces the cause to a single physical factor (nutrition), ignoring the chapter's broader explanation linking emotional changes to the hormonal changes of adolescence and its multi-dimensional well-being framework.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misclassifies emotional change as a physical change, demonstrating a failure to distinguish the chapter's two separate domains — physical changes and emotional and behavioural changes.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are experiencing similar emotions may find this question personally resonant; allow brief reflection before answering. Students may also explain their reasoning verbally rather than in writing if needed.

assessment_items.question_text: An adolescent girl's doctor tells her she has low haemoglobin levels. Which food combination from the chapter would most directly address the nutritional deficiency causing this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Carbohydrates and fats, because the chapter states these are the nutrients most needed during adolescence for energy and strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Milk, curd, and paneer, because these are the chapter's main protein sources for adolescents.

options.label: C
options.text: Millets and cheese, because these are the chapter's primary sources of calcium required for bone development.

options.label: D
options.text: Spinach, kidney beans, and dried fruits, because the chapter identifies these as sources of iron, which is essential for blood formation.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses calcium sources (milk, curd, paneer) with iron sources — a within-chapter confusion between two nutritional categories the chapter distinguishes clearly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly identifies calcium sources from the chapter but misapplies them to a blood-related deficiency rather than bone growth — demonstrating partial chapter knowledge without accurate application.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects macronutrients (carbohydrates and fats) in response to a micronutrient deficiency (iron), showing the student has noted the chapter's nutritional content but cannot match specific nutrients to specific biological functions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unfamiliar with the foods listed may struggle with cultural resonance; teachers may accept equivalent iron-rich foods not listed in the chapter if students can explain the iron connection. The reasoning chain is the assessment target, not food-name recall.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that puberty, the menstrual cycle, and mood changes during adolescence are all primarily driven by the same mechanism. Which statement most accurately describes this mechanism and its reach?

options.label: A
options.text: Hormones are chemical substances produced in different parts of the body, released on signals from the brain, regulating growth, reproduction, and behaviour — making them the common cause of physical, reproductive, and emotional changes during adolescence.

options.label: B
options.text: Hormones are produced only during puberty and stop being released once the body reaches adulthood, which is why the changes they cause are temporary.

options.label: C
options.text: Hormones regulate physical changes like height and voice, but mood swings during adolescence are caused by social pressures rather than any biological mechanism.

options.label: D
options.text: The brain directly controls each change separately — height is controlled by one part of the brain, the menstrual cycle by another, and mood by a third — so there is no single shared mechanism.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Rejects the unifying hormonal mechanism, replacing it with a fragmented brain-control model — shows the student has not engaged with section 6.5's key claim that hormones are the shared driver.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Partially accepts the hormonal mechanism for physical changes but excludes emotional changes, reproducing a common misconception that mood swings are purely social — directly contradicted by the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the heightened hormonal activity of adolescence with a claim that hormones are only produced during that period, misreading the chapter's developmental framing.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who reason well but find abstract mechanism language difficult may draw a simple diagram showing brain → hormone → change (physical / reproductive / emotional) as an equivalent demonstration before selecting the written option.

assessment_items.question_text: The Menstrual Hygiene Scheme (MHS) and the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan are both government programmes mentioned in the chapter. What is the most accurate statement about the biological reasoning behind both schemes?

options.label: A
options.text: Both schemes address the same biological vulnerability — iron deficiency in adolescent girls — because iron is needed for both menstrual health and resistance to addiction.

options.label: B
options.text: Both schemes are social welfare measures with no direct connection to the biological changes of adolescence described in the chapter.

options.label: C
options.text: MHS responds to the biological change of menstruation by supporting hygiene practices, while Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan responds to the vulnerability of adolescence to addiction by promoting awareness — each addressing a distinct biological or health risk of this developmental stage.

options.label: D
options.text: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan targets only adults above 19, so it is not relevant to the biological changes of adolescence covered in the chapter.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Incorrectly conflates the biological rationale of two distinct schemes by forcing a single nutrient (iron) to explain both — showing the student has not traced each scheme to its specific biological basis.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Dismisses the causal link between biology and policy entirely, failing to apply the chapter's framework that each scheme exists because adolescence creates a specific health vulnerability.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misreads the chapter's content on the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, which explicitly targets early-age children and adolescents — demonstrating a recall error rather than an analytical one.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unfamiliar with government scheme names may reason from the biological need alone — 'which scheme addresses menstruation? which addresses addiction?' — as an equivalent analytical pathway.

assessment_items.question_text: A student argues: 'The changes of adolescence are just physical — taller, stronger, louder voice. The emotional changes and the need for special food and hygiene are unrelated to the biology.' Using evidence from the chapter, write a response that evaluates this claim, addressing whether physical, emotional, and well-being changes share a common biological cause.
look_for: Correctly identifies hormones as the common biological cause linking physical changes (height, voice, body structure), reproductive changes (menstrual cycle), and emotional changes (mood swings) — citing section 6.5 explicitly or by content.
Challenges the claim that emotional changes are unrelated to biology by referencing the chapter's statement that mood changes during adolescence are primarily driven by hormonal activity.

Connects well-being measures (nutrition, hygiene, exercise) to the biological changes they support — e.g., iron supports blood formation during menstruation; hygiene addresses changes in armpits and pubic region caused by hormonal activity.

Evaluates the original claim as partially correct (physical changes are real) but fundamentally incomplete, because it misses the shared hormonal mechanism and the biological basis of emotional and well-being needs.
The response draws on at least two domains (physical, emotional, or well-being) with chapter-grounded evidence rather than general statements.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult may structure their response as a point-by-point list (claim / evidence against / conclusion) rather than continuous prose — the quality of biological reasoning, not writing fluency, is the assessment target. Students who draw an annotated causal diagram instead of writing may do so if the diagram shows the hormonal link across all three domains.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Change or challenge described | Biological root (hormonal cause) | Type of change (physical / reproductive / emotional) | Well-being measure from chapter | Biological reason this measure helps
Scenario 1 | Arjun, 13, has developed acne on his face and feels embarrassed | | | |
Scenario 2 | Meera, 12, has begun her menstrual cycle and notices fatigue | | | |
Scenario 3 | Rajan, 14, has been offered cigarettes by older students and feels pressured | | | |
Scenario 4 | Sana, 13, has intense mood swings and withdraws from friends | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each scenario: (1) identify the hormonal or biological root of the change or challenge described, (2) classify the type of change as physical, reproductive, or emotional, (3) name at least one well-being measure from the chapter that addresses it, and (4) explain in the final column why that measure helps, connecting it to the biological change.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row, ask yourself: what is happening in the body to cause this? Is it a physical, reproductive, or emotional change? What does the chapter say an adolescent should do or eat or avoid in this situation, and why does that help biologically?
format_of_output: Completed table with all five columns filled for each of the four scenarios
A brief justification sentence in the final column for each row connecting the measure to the biological cause

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage implied LO requires students to both describe hormonal causes and identify well-being measures — the classification table is the most direct vehicle for demonstrating both simultaneously across multiple domains.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can trace each adolescent situation to its hormonal biological root, classify the type of change accurately, and select and justify a chapter-specific well-being measure — integrating the chapter's causal and practical dimensions in a single analysis.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students through the causal chain (what is happening in the body → what type of change is it → what measure helps → why does it help). Teachers should look for whether students complete the final 'why' column with chapter-grounded reasoning or with general common sense — the final column is the primary discriminator between strong and weak responses.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: correctly names the hormonal mechanism for each scenario (e.g., increased oily secretions for acne; hormonal activity for mood swings; body undergoing rapid change for substance vulnerability); selects a specific chapter measure (e.g., iron from spinach for Meera's fatigue; saying no and seeking support for Rajan); explains the biological link in the final column with reference to chapter content. Weak: fills the table with general health advice not drawn from the chapter; describes the change without tracing it to a hormonal cause; leaves the final column blank or repeats the measure rather than explaining why it helps.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with writing may complete the table using key words and phrases rather than full sentences — the reasoning chain in the final column is the target, not sentence construction. Students who find the four-scenario scope large may complete two rows fully rather than four rows partially, demonstrating the same analytical depth.
